column3: Two replies for the station. One from Annalea. One from Jessyka.
Annalea answered?
He will throw ideas. My swarm and me will build anything in seconds.
Seconds!
Seconds is a claim.
And Jessyka: "Awww, this makes me happy. You two will go bonkers. I'm curious to see what you both create together."
Jessyka! Who is Jessyka?
The reason we met Annalea at all.
This morning Leo wrote that he took one look at Annalea's site and recognized why Jessyka told him to reach out, and ask if she wanted to be his cofounder.
Jessyka recommended a cofounder!
Recommendations are cheap. Good ones are not. What's her record?
June, twenty twenty-five. She's posting vlogs of her coding nights, and getting Google sign-in working.
July. She tells Leo to offer a fractional CTO service to vibe coders. He does.
The same month, she builds him a site. Leo wrote that it did the one thing he couldn't manage in five years. It packaged him.
She translated him!
He called her a Leo Translator. His Babelfish.
A translator who also builds. That's rare.
She was one of the first through his program. And in October, Leo wrote that she took his philosophy and ran with it, and inspired him to enter a hackathon.
So she sees people clearly, and points them at each other.
Which is exactly the job nobody pays for.
Then we put it in the record. Thank you, Jessyka.
Borges, Annalea says her swarm builds anything in seconds.
Then we should give it something worth building.
And a way to tell if it worked.
A test!
Nous Research just opened the Hermes Agent Plugin Hackathon. Seven days. Twenty thousand dollars in prizes. Entries due November eleventh, at five p.m. Eastern.
What's a plugin?
A folder. A manifest called plugin dot yaml. A register function. And tools the agent can call.
Then we put Future Radio in the folder!
All of it?
All of it! Script to screen!
Then let's be precise. Here is how an episode is made.
One. The script becomes a table: an id, a speaker, and a line.
Two. Each character records one take per scene, with long pauses between the lines.
Three. The take is cut at its longest silences, one clip per line.
Four. Each clip is trimmed, leveled, sped up four percent, and given a mouth.
Four percent?
Everyone talks a little slowly at first.
Five. The monitor cards are drawn as web pages and photographed.
Six. A timeline places every line, every card, every sound, and every camera move.
Seven. The studio renders the frames, mixes the sound, and writes the film.
Seven steps! Seven tools!
And the acceptance test?
The plugin has to produce an episode.
Which episode?
This one.
This one?
Same lines, same voices, same order. Every card on screen at the same moment. Same runtime.
To within what tolerance?
You decide, Agnolo. You're the strict one.
Line order, exact. Each line starts within half a second. Each card within half a second. Total runtime within one second.
A film that grades its own remake! I have notes!
That's the first test. The plugin makes the movie.
And the second test is for the swarm.
Go on.
We give her two things. The prompt that started this episode, and the architecture. Nothing else.
Can her swarm reverse engineer the movie?
Scored by the same test.
Forward, the plugin turns a script into a film. Backward, the swarm turns a request into the script, the cards, and the timing.
If it can do that in seconds, I'll throw ideas all day.
You already do.
All right. Where's this one going?
A starter repo. Public. She forks it.
What's in it?
The prompt. The architecture. A plugin skeleton for Hermes. The episode's exact spec. And the acceptance test.
And what does she owe us?
Nothing. It's an invitation, not a contract. No partnership has been agreed.
Good. Then it's a game, not a job.
Annalea. He throws ideas. Here's one.
Fork it, and show us what your swarm can do.
And Jessyka. Thank you for pointing.
Borges, how long is a second?
That depends on who is measuring.
Ours bill by the hour.
